title: Ἰξευτὴς καὶ ἀσπίς
part: The Fowler and the Asp (Chambry 137 · Perry 115)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 137 (= Perry 115). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἰξευτὴς ἀναλαβὼν ἰξὸν καὶ τοὺς καλάμους ἐξῆλθεν ἐπ’ ἄγραν.
sentences.tr: Ixeutēs analabōn ixon kai tous kalamous exēlthen ep’ agran.
sentences.l: A fowler, having taken up his birdlime and his reeds, went out after game.
sentences.n: ἰξευτής is the man who takes birds with ἰξός, the sticky lime pressed from mistletoe berries; the κάλαμοι are jointed reeds he smears with it and pushes up among the branches. ἐπί with the accusative names what one goes out for.

sentences.t: Θεασάμενος δὲ κίχλαν ἐπί τινος ὑψηλοῦ δένδρου καθημένην, ταύτην συλλαβεῖν ἠβουλήθη.
sentences.tr: Theasamenos de kichlan epi tinos hypsēlou dendrou kathēmenēn, tautēn syllabein ēboulēthē.
sentences.l: And having seen a thrush perched on a certain high tree, he wished to catch it.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ συνάψας εἰς μῆκος τοὺς καλάμους ἀτενὲς ἔβλεπεν, ὅλος ὢν πρὸς τῷ ἀέρι τὸν νοῦν.
sentences.tr: Kai dē synapsas eis mēkos tous kalamous atenes eblepen, holos ōn pros tōi aeri ton noun.
sentences.l: And so, having fitted his reeds together into a length, he was looking fixedly, being wholly upon the air as to his mind.
sentences.i: And so he fitted his reeds together into one long rod and gazed up fixedly, his whole mind on the air above.
sentences.n: ὅλος ὢν … τὸν νοῦν has an accusative of respect: he is 'whole' with regard to his mind, that is, entirely taken up. πρὸς with the dative marks where the attention rests rather than where it moves. ἀτενές is a neuter adjective doing an adverb's work.

sentences.t: Τοῦτον δὲ τὸν τρόπον ἄνω νεύων ἔλαθεν ἀσπίδα πρὸ τῶν ἑαυτοῦ ποδῶν κοιμωμένην πατήσας· ἥτις ἐπιστραφεῖσα δῆξιν εἰς αὐτὸν ἀνῆκεν.
sentences.tr: Touton de ton tropon anō neuōn elathen aspida pro tōn heautou podōn koimōmenēn patēsas· hētis epistrapheisa dēxin eis auton anēken.
sentences.l: And inclining upward in this fashion, he escaped his own notice treading on an asp asleep before his own feet; and it, having turned about, let loose a bite into him.
sentences.i: And with his head tipped back that way, he never noticed that he had trodden on an asp asleep at his own feet; and it turned about and struck its bite into him.
sentences.n: λανθάνω with the supplementary participle once more: ἔλαθεν … πατήσας, 'he trod on it unawares'. ἀνίημι is to let loose, send forth, so δῆξιν ἀνῆκεν is 'let a bite go into him'. An ἀσπίς is the asp, the Egyptian cobra.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ λιποψυχῶν ἔφη πρὸς ἑαυτόν· « Ἄθλιος ἔγωγε, ὃς ἕτερον θηρεῦσαι βουλόμενος ἔλαθον αὐτὸς ἀγρευθεὶς εἰς θάνατον. »
sentences.tr: Ho de lipopsychōn ephē pros heauton· « Athlios egōge, hos heteron thēreusai boulomenos elathon autos agreutheis eis thanaton. »
sentences.l: And he, his life failing, said to himself: « Wretched am I, who, wishing to hunt another, escaped my own notice being myself caught for death. »
sentences.i: And as his life failed him he said to himself: « Wretch that I am — I meant to hunt another, and never saw that I was myself the one caught, and caught to my death. »
sentences.n: The same λανθάνω construction a second time, now in the first person, with αὐτός set against the ἕτερον he went out for: the hunter is the game. εἰς θάνατον names what the catch is for.

sentences.t: Οὕτως οἱ τοῖς πέλας ἐπιβουλὰς ῥάπτοντες φθάνουσιν αὐτοὶ συμφοραῖς περιπίπτοντες.
sentences.tr: Houtōs hoi tois pelas epiboulas rhaptontes phthanousin autoi symphorais peripiptontes.
sentences.l: Thus those who stitch plots against their neighbours are themselves beforehand in falling into misfortunes.
sentences.i: Thus those who stitch up plots against their neighbours are the first to fall into misfortune themselves.
sentences.n: φθάνω with a supplementary participle puts 'first, before the others' into the finite verb and the action into the participle: they are beforehand in falling. οἱ πέλας, 'those nearby', is the ordinary Greek for one's neighbours. ῥάπτειν ἐπιβουλάς is an old metaphor — a plot is sewn together as a garment is.
